content.value: A field-tested audit of one real Windows onboarding journey across Barkpark Cloud, multi-team identity, a custom instance hostname, Codex/Cursor MCP, Studio access, and the follow-on publication journey to the Guerrilla Barkpark.
Windows · Gyldendal onboarding · Guerrilla publishing · multi-team identity · Codex/Cursor MCP · Portable Docs
The onboarding eventually succeeded: a Windows user authenticated through Barkpark Cloud, selected a second team where they were an administrator, retrieved the correct instance credential, connected
bp
to
https://gyldendal.barkpark.cloud
, registered the MCP server for Codex and Cursor, completed a live MCP handshake, called
task_ready
, published a paper, read it back, and rendered it over HTTPS.

The successful path was not discoverable from the product surface. It required maintainer-level diagnosis across Cloud account, Cloud team, instance-local account, API bearer, three instance URLs, two teams, a direct team-scoped request, and a Windows CLI compatibility workaround.
The underlying security and APIs are mostly sound; the onboarding composition is not.

blocks.text: Publishing the audit to Guerrilla: the second onboarding journey

items.value: The Guerrilla server already existed as a saved CLI target with a credential; this session did not exercise a brand-new Guerrilla login.
bp -s Guerrilla whoami confirmed https://guerrilla.barkpark.cloud was reachable and authenticated at admin tier, while also reporting active: false because Gyldendal remained the default target.
Every Guerrilla read and write therefore required an explicit -s Guerrilla selector; omitting it would have sent the operation to the active Gyldendal instance.
The first audit was authored as body_html, the legacy fallback. The publish wall required a non-trivial description and a weighted spine using tags registered on the Guerrilla instance.
The first successful Guerrilla publish produced revision 1 and a possible-duplicate warning against another paper with similarity 0.4118, but supplied no direct compare or review action.
Revision 2 added the discovered HTML/CLI parity failure. HTTP and browser read-back worked; bp paper view failed with has no renderable blocks.
The rendered audit was structurally complete but visually flat because raw HTML bypassed Portable Doc article chrome and semantic components. This was noticed only through human visual review.

Source inspection established that blocks are the preferred source of truth and body_html is explicitly legacy. The Bulldocs manifest exposes publish and patch, but no get/list/export command for retrieving the current block document.

Migration required fetching the public rendered HTML and running the repository converter. A normal
void element caused the converter to silently emit 2 blocks instead of the expected 57 until the source was normalized to
.
The first native-block publish was rejected as malformed because --file replaces the entire request body: the required positional slug was discarded and had to be duplicated inside the JSON payload.

The next publish reached the label spine but failed because the weighted tag objects used name/weight rather than the required tag/strength/rationale fields. The rejection hint was useful; a preflight schema would have prevented the round trip.
After correcting the slug and label schema, revision 3 published as 64+ native components and bp paper view, HTTP read-back, and the web renderer all converged.

blocks.caption: The missing composition layer: one identity transaction feeds three user-facing surfaces.
blocks.source:
flowchart LR
  A["Cloud account"] --> B["Team context"]
  B --> C["Instance identity + aliases"]
  C --> D["Credential + CLI config"]
  D --> E["Codex / Cursor MCP"]
  D --> F["Studio"]
  D --> G["Portable Docs"]

blocks.text: 1. Identity planes are secure but not composed

content.value: Barkpark Cloud sessions manage teams and fleets. Instance bearer tokens authorize content APIs. Studio can also have local account/password authentication. Enterprise SSO is a fourth option. Each boundary is defensible, but onboarding presents them as one “Barkpark login” concept. The user cannot predict which credential applies to which surface.

Multi-team membership is visible in the Cloud console and supported by team-scoped APIs, but the installed CLI session carries one default team. Commands that operate on instance IDs do not consistently accept or infer a team. Privacy-preserving 404 behavior then hides the actual fix.

blocks.text: 3. Instance identity is represented by URL strings

content.value: The same instance has a canonical generated hostname and a short custom hostname. Credentials and saved-server matching follow URL identity, so an alias behaves like a different server until separately registered. Instance ID should be the durable key.

blocks.text: 4. Release, documentation, and server capabilities move at different speeds

content.value: The live server, repository documentation, Windows binary, installer, and MCP catalog did not describe the same product wave. The manifest-driven architecture is designed to reduce this drift, but built-in/onramp behavior and release packaging remain version-sensitive.

blocks.text: 5. Health and success signals are fragmented

content.value: Cloud fleet health, agent status, API reachability, Studio reachability, authentication tier, and MCP readiness are separate signals. The user saw “down” or “agent offline” while the useful paths worked. Onboarding needs one diagnostic that explains each layer rather than a single status adjective.

blocks.text: 6. Paper write and read paths do not share one canonical representation

content.value: The publish path accepts and renders
body_html
, while
bp paper view
requires renderable blocks. A successful write can therefore fail its own CLI read-back check. Accepted authoring formats need either symmetric readers or deterministic normalization at publish time.

blocks.text: 7. Portable document authoring is not the default path

content.value: The publish API accepts both native blocks and raw body_html, but the legacy fallback is easier to reach than the preferred component model. The result can be publishable yet visually generic, difficult to edit, and unreadable by terminal tooling. The preferred format needs first-class examples, conversion, and linting.

blocks.text: 8. File payload precedence breaks the declared command contract

content.value: The publish manifest requires a positional slug, but the generic CLI body builder lets --file override the entire request body. Because the publish route has no slug path segment, the positional value disappears and the JSON must repeat it. The CLI should compose declared arguments with file payloads instead of silently discarding them.

blocks.text: 9. Write-target context is selectable but not ambiently visible

content.value: The saved-server selector works, but a command aimed at Guerrilla can coexist with a different active server. That is safe only when every command repeats -s Guerrilla. Cross-tenant writes need a persistent, conspicuous target context and receipts that make an active/explicit mismatch impossible to overlook.

blocks.text: 10. The publishing contract is distributed across too many surfaces

content.value: Portable block shapes live in the renderer and SDK, label-spine rules live in the publish wall, registered tags live on the instance, file precedence lives in the generic CLI, and conversion lives in a repository script. A maintainer must assemble the complete contract from implementation details and rejection messages.

blocks.text: Acceptance criteria for a production-quality onboarding

items.value: A clean Windows machine installs the newest supported CLI from the documented command.
The installer verifies checksum, updates PATH, and proves
bp version
from a fresh process environment.
A multi-team user can select the intended team during login or immediately afterward.
The CLI lists every authorized instance with team ownership and health dimensions.
A custom hostname and canonical hostname resolve to one saved instance and one token.
A Cloud admin can enter Studio without creating a separate local account or pasting an API token.
bp instance credentials
works for any authorized team without direct REST.
Codex and Cursor onramps are idempotent and preserve unrelated configuration.
The documented curated MCP tool count exactly matches the launched server or emits a version warning.
A read-only MCP smoke succeeds in under 30 seconds.
No step requires viewing, copying, or committing a raw credential.
The complete path takes under five minutes for a first-time user and under two minutes for an existing Cloud user.
Every accepted paper body format passes publish,
bp paper view
, API read-back, and web-render parity checks.
The default paper workflow emits block-backed Portable Docs with article chrome and component-level CLI/API/web parity.
Every write preview and receipt names the exact server, workspace, project, and whether an explicit selector differs from the active target.
Publish preflight validates block schema, label spine, registered tags, duplicate candidates, and lossy conversion before any revision is written.
A published paper can be listed, exported as canonical blocks, compared, read in the CLI, and opened on the web from one coherent command family.
A required positional slug is honored when --file is used; authors never duplicate command arguments inside payload JSON.

blocks.source:
flowchart LR

blocks.text: 1. Identity planes are secure but not composed

content.value: Barkpark Cloud sessions manage teams and fleets. Instance bearer tokens authorize content APIs. Studio can also have local account/password authentication. Enterprise SSO is a fourth option. Each boundary is defensible, but onboarding presents them as one “Barkpark login” concept. The user cannot predict which credential applies to which surface.

Multi-team membership is visible in the Cloud console and supported by team-scoped APIs, but the installed CLI session carries one default team. Commands that operate on instance IDs do not consistently accept or infer a team. Privacy-preserving 404 behavior then hides the actual fix.

blocks.text: 3. Instance identity is represented by URL strings

content.value: The same instance has a canonical generated hostname and a short custom hostname. Credentials and saved-server matching follow URL identity, so an alias behaves like a different server until separately registered. Instance ID should be the durable key.

blocks.text: 4. Release, documentation, and server capabilities move at different speeds

content.value: The live server, repository documentation, Windows binary, installer, and MCP catalog did not describe the same product wave. The manifest-driven architecture is designed to reduce this drift, but built-in/onramp behavior and release packaging remain version-sensitive.

blocks.text: 5. Health and success signals are fragmented

content.value: Cloud fleet health, agent status, API reachability, Studio reachability, authentication tier, and MCP readiness are separate signals. The user saw “down” or “agent offline” while the useful paths worked. Onboarding needs one diagnostic that explains each layer rather than a single status adjective.

blocks.text: 6. Paper write and read paths do not share one canonical representation

content.value: The publish path accepts and renders
body_html
, while
bp paper view
requires renderable blocks. A successful write can therefore fail its own CLI read-back check. Accepted authoring formats need either symmetric readers or deterministic normalization at publish time.

blocks.text: 7. Portable document authoring is not the default path

content.value: The publish API accepts both native blocks and raw body_html, but the legacy fallback is easier to reach than the preferred component model. The result can be publishable yet visually generic, difficult to edit, and unreadable by terminal tooling. The preferred format needs first-class examples, conversion, and linting.

blocks.text: 8. File payload precedence breaks the declared command contract

content.value: The publish manifest requires a positional slug, but the generic CLI body builder lets --file override the entire request body. Because the publish route has no slug path segment, the positional value disappears and the JSON must repeat it. The CLI should compose declared arguments with file payloads instead of silently discarding them.

blocks.text: 9. Write-target context is selectable but not ambiently visible

content.value: The saved-server selector works, but a command aimed at Guerrilla can coexist with a different active server. That is safe only when every command repeats -s Guerrilla. Cross-tenant writes need a persistent, conspicuous target context and receipts that make an active/explicit mismatch impossible to overlook.

blocks.text: 10. The publishing contract is distributed across too many surfaces

content.value: Portable block shapes live in the renderer and SDK, label-spine rules live in the publish wall, registered tags live on the instance, file precedence lives in the generic CLI, and conversion lives in a repository script. A maintainer must assemble the complete contract from implementation details and rejection messages.

BARKPARK MAINTAINER FIELD REPORT

Barkpark onboarding pain-point audit

A field-tested audit of one real Windows onboarding journey across Barkpark Cloud, multi-team identity, a custom instance hostname, Codex/Cursor MCP, Studio access, and the follow-on publication journey to the Guerrilla Barkpark.

13 July 2026 · Barkpark maintainers · Revision 5 · Sensitive evidence redacted

Scope
Windows · Gyldendal onboarding · Guerrilla publishing · multi-team identity · Codex/Cursor MCP · Portable Docs

Executive summary

The onboarding eventually succeeded: a Windows user authenticated through Barkpark Cloud, selected a second team where they were an administrator, retrieved the correct instance credential, connected bp to https://gyldendal.barkpark.cloud, registered the MCP server for Codex and Cursor, completed a live MCP handshake, called task_ready, published a paper, read it back, and rendered it over HTTPS.

Why this matters
The successful path was not discoverable from the product surface. It required maintainer-level diagnosis across Cloud account, Cloud team, instance-local account, API bearer, three instance URLs, two teams, a direct team-scoped request, and a Windows CLI compatibility workaround.

The underlying security and APIs are mostly sound; the onboarding composition is not.

Outcome and proof

• Cloud device authorization completed without exposing a password or bearer token to the CLI transcript.
• The account was confirmed as an administrator of the intended Gyldendal team.
• bp whoami reported the short hostname as active, reachable, and authenticated at admin tier.
• MCP protocol 2025-06-18 initialized successfully.
• The installed client exposed five task tools: task_close, task_create, task_next, task_ready, and task_show.
• A read-only task_ready call returned live Gyldendal tasks.
• A proof paper was published, read back in the terminal, fetched with HTTP 200, and visually rendered.
Verified outcome
Cloud authorization, team selection, instance setup, MCP initialize/tools/list/task_ready, paper publish, HTTP read-back, and browser rendering all succeeded without exposing credentials.

Environment

The intended happy path

1. Install the current bp release.
2. Run bp login --device and approve in Barkpark Cloud.
3. Select the correct team and instance from every authorized membership.
4. Connect the CLI to the instance; custom and canonical hostnames resolve to the same instance identity.
5. Run bp onramp codex --write and/or bp onramp cursor --write.
6. Reload the client and see the curated task tools.
7. Verify with one read-only tool call.

This should be a two-to-five-minute journey with no raw token handling, direct REST calls, manual JSON edits, DNS investigation, or product-source inspection.

Actual journey: evidence timeline

1. The CLI existed but was not on the user PATH. The binary was present under the Windows local-app-data Barkpark directory, while Get-Command bp initially failed. MCP configs using command = "bp" would therefore fail after client launch.
2. The repository already contained partial Barkpark instructions but no MCP registration. A Cursor task rule existed, while Codex and Cursor MCP config files were absent. The host repository also had a separate task-tracker contract, creating governance ambiguity outside Barkpark itself.
3. The current documentation described capabilities the installed binary did not have. The docs recommended bp onramp codex --write; the installed build replied that --write was a later wave and the command was print-only.
4. Codex and Cursor were configured manually. Project-local files were used so unrelated global settings were not touched. Token material was intentionally omitted.
5. The first MCP proof worked, but only exposed five tools. Current documentation describes eight curated tools, including task_prime, task_stamp, and task_pulse. The installed Windows build exposed the older five-tool catalog.
6. Updating the CLI failed on Windows. The official installer resolved cli-v1.14.0 and attempted to download bp-windows-amd64.exe. That release contains Darwin and Linux assets plus checksums, but no Windows asset. The installer stopped with a generic download failure.
7. The requested short hostname was not the existing saved instance. gyldendal.barkpark.cloud and gyldendal-506f035e.barkpark.cloud resolved to different servers. Reusing the old instance token against the short hostname correctly yielded anonymous tier / token rejection.
8. Anonymous capability discovery produced a misleading CLI symptom. Against the short hostname without a matching saved token, bp task ready returned unknown command "task" "ready". The real problem was missing authentication/context, not an unsupported command.
9. The production capabilities envelope identified itself with a localhost base URL. Anonymous capabilities from the short hostname reported base_url: http://localhost:4000, auth_tier: none, and no task noun. Even if base URL is informational, this strongly suggests a deployment/configuration leak and makes remote diagnosis harder.
10. Cloud user access and Studio user access looked interchangeable but were not. The short-host Studio showed an instance-local email/password form, token login, and enterprise SSO hint. The maintainer reasonably expected their Barkpark Cloud admin account to work; the local login rejected it and led into password recovery. Root-cause map

1. Identity planes are secure but not composed

Barkpark Cloud sessions manage teams and fleets. Instance bearer tokens authorize content APIs. Studio can also have local account/password authentication. Enterprise SSO is a fourth option. Each boundary is defensible, but onboarding presents them as one “Barkpark login” concept. The user cannot predict which credential applies to which surface.

2. Team context is implicit

Multi-team membership is visible in the Cloud console and supported by team-scoped APIs, but the installed CLI session carries one default team. Commands that operate on instance IDs do not consistently accept or infer a team. Privacy-preserving 404 behavior then hides the actual fix.

3. Instance identity is represented by URL strings

The same instance has a canonical generated hostname and a short custom hostname. Credentials and saved-server matching follow URL identity, so an alias behaves like a different server until separately registered. Instance ID should be the durable key.

4. Release, documentation, and server capabilities move at different speeds

The live server, repository documentation, Windows binary, installer, and MCP catalog did not describe the same product wave. The manifest-driven architecture is designed to reduce this drift, but built-in/onramp behavior and release packaging remain version-sensitive.

5. Health and success signals are fragmented

Cloud fleet health, agent status, API reachability, Studio reachability, authentication tier, and MCP readiness are separate signals. The user saw “down” or “agent offline” while the useful paths worked. Onboarding needs one diagnostic that explains each layer rather than a single status adjective.

6. Paper write and read paths do not share one canonical representation

The publish path accepts and renders body_html, while bp paper view requires renderable blocks. A successful write can therefore fail its own CLI read-back check. Accepted authoring formats need either symmetric readers or deterministic normalization at publish time.

7. Portable document authoring is not the default path

The publish API accepts both native blocks and raw body_html, but the legacy fallback is easier to reach than the preferred component model. The result can be publishable yet visually generic, difficult to edit, and unreadable by terminal tooling. The preferred format needs first-class examples, conversion, and linting.

8. File payload precedence breaks the declared command contract

The publish manifest requires a positional slug, but the generic CLI body builder lets --file override the entire request body. Because the publish route has no slug path segment, the positional value disappears and the JSON must repeat it. The CLI should compose declared arguments with file payloads instead of silently discarding them.

9. Write-target context is selectable but not ambiently visible

The saved-server selector works, but a command aimed at Guerrilla can coexist with a different active server. That is safe only when every command repeats -s Guerrilla. Cross-tenant writes need a persistent, conspicuous target context and receipts that make an active/explicit mismatch impossible to overlook.

10. The publishing contract is distributed across too many surfaces

Portable block shapes live in the renderer and SDK, label-spine rules live in the publish wall, registered tags live on the instance, file precedence lives in the generic CLI, and conversion lives in a repository script. A maintainer must assemble the complete contract from implementation details and rejection messages.

What worked well

• Device authorization security: single-use code, explicit device/IP/client display, Approve/Deny choice, and no password in the CLI.
• Scoped privacy behavior: cross-team credential lookup returned the same not-found shape as a nonexistent instance.
• Team-scoped API exists: X-Barkpark-Team and GetCredentialsForTeam already provide most of the needed backend contract.
• bp whoami is strong: it exposed active target, source, reachability, auth tier, scope, and Cloud team without revealing tokens.
• MCP transport was reliable: byte-clean initialize/tools/list/tool-call flow, authenticated live read, and clean EOF shutdown.
• Project-local client configs worked: Codex and Cursor could be configured without touching unrelated global settings.
• Paper write/read/render closed the loop: a real external mutation and independent read-back proved the connection beyond a config-only check.
• The Portable Doc renderer already provides semantic article chrome, callouts, sections, diagrams, tables, and cross-surface rendering.

Recommended product changes

P0 — make the golden path possible
1. Gate releases on Windows assets. CI must fail a CLI release unless Darwin, Linux, and Windows binaries plus checksum entries exist for every supported architecture.
2. Make team selection first-class. Add bp teams, bp team use <name|id>, bp login --team, and a team selector on device approval when the account has multiple memberships.
3. Fix instance credential routing. Add bp instance credentials <id> --team <name|id> and route through GetCredentialsForTeam. If no team is supplied, search authorized memberships and succeed only on one unambiguous match.
4. Bridge Cloud to Studio. Put “Continue with Barkpark Cloud” on the instance login page or redirect Cloud-managed instances through a signed, short-lived Studio link. Clearly label local account and API-token alternatives.
P1 — make the path obvious and diagnosable
1. Identify instances by ID, not URL. Store canonical URL plus aliases under one instance record and one credential.
2. Ship bp doctor onboarding. It should test PATH, binary/release freshness, Cloud session, team memberships, target instance, canonical/alias DNS, credential availability, API/Studio health, Tasks plugin, MCP catalog, and client config.
3. Version the onramps. Docs should state the minimum CLI version per feature. The CLI should print an exact upgrade requirement instead of accepting an unknown documented flag.
4. Improve command-discovery errors. Distinguish unsupported command, hidden-by-auth command, plugin-disabled command, and stale manifest cache.
5. Decompose fleet health. Render Agent, API, Studio, and last golden-path probe as separate fields with timestamps.
6. Make block-backed Portable Docs the default; warn on body_html-only publishing and provide a one-command converter.
P2 — remove recovery friction
1. Accept UTF-8 BOM in config JSON.
2. Offer a stable non-interactive device-flow protocol that emits start data immediately and polls separately.
3. Make setup output collision-proof: team, instance ID prefix, saved name, canonical URL, aliases, active state.
4. Have onramp doctor detect conflicting repository instructions and pre-existing MCP stanzas before writing.
5. Guarantee paper write/read parity: every format accepted by publish must be readable through CLI, API, and web renderers.

Authoring conclusion
Portable components are not decoration. They are the shared semantic contract that makes a paper styled, editable, streamable, accessible, and readable across the web, CLI, and future clients.

Barkpark already has the hard parts: secure device authorization, team-scoped backend contracts, manifest-driven capabilities, a useful whoami, reliable MCP transport, and a paper surface that proves live writes. The onboarding failure came from missing composition between those parts.

The highest-leverage change is to make team + instance + alias + credential + client onramp one explicit transaction. If Barkpark can produce one trustworthy receipt for that transaction—and ship the same CLI wave on Windows that the docs describe—the journey becomes both shorter and safer.

  3. Every Guerrilla read and write therefore required an explicit -s Guerrilla selector; omitting it would have sent the operation to the active Gyldendal instance.
  4. The first audit was authored as body_html, the legacy fallback. The publish wall required a non-trivial description and a weighted spine using tags registered on the Guerrilla instance.
  5. The first successful Guerrilla publish produced revision 1 and a possible-duplicate warning against another paper with similarity 0.4118, but supplied no direct compare or review action.
  6. Revision 2 added the discovered HTML/CLI parity failure. HTTP and browser read-back worked; bp paper view failed with has no renderable blocks.
  7. The rendered audit was structurally complete but visually flat because raw HTML bypassed Portable Doc article chrome and semantic components. This was noticed only through human visual review.
  8. Source inspection established that blocks are the preferred source of truth and body_html is explicitly legacy. The Bulldocs manifest exposes publish and patch, but no get/list/export command for retrieving the current block document.
  9. Migration required fetching the public rendered HTML and running the repository converter. A normal <br> void element caused the converter to silently emit 2 blocks instead of the expected 57 until the source was normalized to <br/>.
  10. The first native-block publish was rejected as malformed because --file replaces the entire request body: the required positional slug was discarded and had to be duplicated inside the JSON payload.
  11. The next publish reached the label spine but failed because the weighted tag objects used name/weight rather than the required tag/strength/rationale fields. The rejection hint was useful; a preflight schema would have prevented the round trip.
  12. After correcting the slug and label schema, revision 3 published as 64+ native components and bp paper view, HTTP read-back, and the web renderer all converged.
Presentation defect discovered during review The first serious audit was authored as raw body_html. It rendered as a flat article, bypassed Portable Doc components and article chrome, and failed bp paper view. The product accepted a legacy fallback without steering the maintainer toward the portable source-of-truth format.

Root-cause map

1. Identity planes are secure but not composed

Barkpark Cloud sessions manage teams and fleets. Instance bearer tokens authorize content APIs. Studio can also have local account/password authentication. Enterprise SSO is a fourth option. Each boundary is defensible, but onboarding presents them as one “Barkpark login” concept. The user cannot predict which credential applies to which surface.

2. Team context is implicit

Multi-team membership is visible in the Cloud console and supported by team-scoped APIs, but the installed CLI session carries one default team. Commands that operate on instance IDs do not consistently accept or infer a team. Privacy-preserving 404 behavior then hides the actual fix.

3. Instance identity is represented by URL strings

The same instance has a canonical generated hostname and a short custom hostname. Credentials and saved-server matching follow URL identity, so an alias behaves like a different server until separately registered. Instance ID should be the durable key.

4. Release, documentation, and server capabilities move at different speeds

The live server, repository documentation, Windows binary, installer, and MCP catalog did not describe the same product wave. The manifest-driven architecture is designed to reduce this drift, but built-in/onramp behavior and release packaging remain version-sensitive.

5. Health and success signals are fragmented

Cloud fleet health, agent status, API reachability, Studio reachability, authentication tier, and MCP readiness are separate signals. The user saw “down” or “agent offline” while the useful paths worked. Onboarding needs one diagnostic that explains each layer rather than a single status adjective.

6. Paper write and read paths do not share one canonical representation

The publish path accepts and renders body_html, while bp paper view requires renderable blocks. A successful write can therefore fail its own CLI read-back check. Accepted authoring formats need either symmetric readers or deterministic normalization at publish time.

7. Portable document authoring is not the default path

The publish API accepts both native blocks and raw body_html, but the legacy fallback is easier to reach than the preferred component model. The result can be publishable yet visually generic, difficult to edit, and unreadable by terminal tooling. The preferred format needs first-class examples, conversion, and linting.

8. File payload precedence breaks the declared command contract

The publish manifest requires a positional slug, but the generic CLI body builder lets --file override the entire request body. Because the publish route has no slug path segment, the positional value disappears and the JSON must repeat it. The CLI should compose declared arguments with file payloads instead of silently discarding them.

9. Write-target context is selectable but not ambiently visible

The saved-server selector works, but a command aimed at Guerrilla can coexist with a different active server. That is safe only when every command repeats -s Guerrilla. Cross-tenant writes need a persistent, conspicuous target context and receipts that make an active/explicit mismatch impossible to overlook.

10. The publishing contract is distributed across too many surfaces

Portable block shapes live in the renderer and SDK, label-spine rules live in the publish wall, registered tags live on the instance, file precedence lives in the generic CLI, and conversion lives in a repository script. A maintainer must assemble the complete contract from implementation details and rejection messages.

What worked well

  • Device authorization security: single-use code, explicit device/IP/client display, Approve/Deny choice, and no password in the CLI.
  • Scoped privacy behavior: cross-team credential lookup returned the same not-found shape as a nonexistent instance.
  • Team-scoped API exists: X-Barkpark-Team and GetCredentialsForTeam already provide most of the needed backend contract.
  • bp whoami is strong: it exposed active target, source, reachability, auth tier, scope, and Cloud team without revealing tokens.
  • MCP transport was reliable: byte-clean initialize/tools/list/tool-call flow, authenticated live read, and clean EOF shutdown.
  • Project-local client configs worked: Codex and Cursor could be configured without touching unrelated global settings.
  • Paper write/read/render closed the loop: a real external mutation and independent read-back proved the connection beyond a config-only check.
  • The Portable Doc renderer already provides semantic article chrome, callouts, sections, diagrams, tables, and cross-surface rendering.

Recommended product changes

P0 — make the golden path possible
  1. Gate releases on Windows assets. CI must fail a CLI release unless Darwin, Linux, and Windows binaries plus checksum entries exist for every supported architecture.
  2. Make team selection first-class. Add bp teams, bp team use <name|id>, bp login --team, and a team selector on device approval when the account has multiple memberships.
  3. Fix instance credential routing. Add bp instance credentials <id> --team <name|id> and route through GetCredentialsForTeam. If no team is supplied, search authorized memberships and succeed only on one unambiguous match.
  4. Bridge Cloud to Studio. Put “Continue with Barkpark Cloud” on the instance login page or redirect Cloud-managed instances through a signed, short-lived Studio link. Clearly label local account and API-token alternatives.
P1 — make the path obvious and diagnosable
  1. Identify instances by ID, not URL. Store canonical URL plus aliases under one instance record and one credential.
  2. Ship bp doctor onboarding. It should test PATH, binary/release freshness, Cloud session, team memberships, target instance, canonical/alias DNS, credential availability, API/Studio health, Tasks plugin, MCP catalog, and client config.
  3. Version the onramps. Docs should state the minimum CLI version per feature. The CLI should print an exact upgrade requirement instead of accepting an unknown documented flag.
  4. Improve command-discovery errors. Distinguish unsupported command, hidden-by-auth command, plugin-disabled command, and stale manifest cache.
  5. Decompose fleet health. Render Agent, API, Studio, and last golden-path probe as separate fields with timestamps.
  6. Make block-backed Portable Docs the default; warn on body_html-only publishing and provide a one-command converter.
P2 — remove recovery friction
  1. Accept UTF-8 BOM in config JSON.
  2. Offer a stable non-interactive device-flow protocol that emits start data immediately and polls separately.
  3. Make setup output collision-proof: team, instance ID prefix, saved name, canonical URL, aliases, active state.
  4. Have onramp doctor detect conflicting repository instructions and pre-existing MCP stanzas before writing.
  5. Guarantee paper write/read parity: every format accepted by publish must be readable through CLI, API, and web renderers.

Proposed single-command journey

bp login --device
# browser approval includes team selection when needed

bp connect cloud --team Gyldendal --instance gyldendal \
  --url https://gyldendal.barkpark.cloud

bp onramp codex --write
bp onramp cursor --write
bp mcp doctor --call task_ready

The final command should return a compact receipt containing target instance ID, team, URL/aliases, auth tier, tool catalog version, tool names, read-only call result, and exact client-reload instruction. It must never print the bearer.

Acceptance criteria for a production-quality onboarding

  1. A clean Windows machine installs the newest supported CLI from the documented command.
  2. The installer verifies checksum, updates PATH, and proves bp version from a fresh process environment.
  3. A multi-team user can select the intended team during login or immediately afterward.
  4. The CLI lists every authorized instance with team ownership and health dimensions.
  5. A custom hostname and canonical hostname resolve to one saved instance and one token.
  6. A Cloud admin can enter Studio without creating a separate local account or pasting an API token.
  7. bp instance credentials works for any authorized team without direct REST.
  8. Codex and Cursor onramps are idempotent and preserve unrelated configuration.
  9. The documented curated MCP tool count exactly matches the launched server or emits a version warning.
  10. A read-only MCP smoke succeeds in under 30 seconds.
  11. No step requires viewing, copying, or committing a raw credential.
  12. The complete path takes under five minutes for a first-time user and under two minutes for an existing Cloud user.
  13. Every accepted paper body format passes publish, bp paper view, API read-back, and web-render parity checks.
  14. The default paper workflow emits block-backed Portable Docs with article chrome and component-level CLI/API/web parity.
  15. Every write preview and receipt names the exact server, workspace, project, and whether an explicit selector differs from the active target.
  16. Publish preflight validates block schema, label spine, registered tags, duplicate candidates, and lossy conversion before any revision is written.
  17. A published paper can be listed, exported as canonical blocks, compared, read in the CLI, and opened on the web from one coherent command family.
  18. A required positional slug is honored when --file is used; authors never duplicate command arguments inside payload JSON.

Suggested backlog slices

  1. Release: restore Windows CLI artifacts and installer contract.
  2. Cloud auth: multi-team device authorization and bp team use.
  3. CLI: team-aware instance credentials via GetCredentialsForTeam.
  4. Studio: Continue with Barkpark Cloud signed-link login.
  5. Config: instance-ID identity with canonical/custom URL aliases.
  6. Doctor: end-to-end onboarding and MCP diagnostic receipt.
  7. Errors: auth-hidden command vs unsupported command classification.
  8. Fleet: split agent/API/Studio health and freshness.
  9. Parser: tolerate UTF-8 BOM.
  10. Docs/release: feature-version matrix and executable examples.
  11. Papers: normalize accepted body formats and add CLI/API/web read-parity tests.
  12. Authoring UX: component cookbook, HTML-to-block conversion, publish lint, and default article preview.
  13. Target safety: persistent server/workspace/project context plus active-vs-explicit mismatch warnings on every write.
  14. Publish UX: preflight command, registered-tag discovery, duplicate comparison, and canonical block export.
  15. Converter safety: correct HTML void-element parsing and fail closed on suspicious content loss.
  16. CLI body composition: retain declared positional/body arguments when loading a JSON file, with explicit conflict rules.

Final assessment

Authoring conclusion Portable components are not decoration. They are the shared semantic contract that makes a paper styled, editable, streamable, accessible, and readable across the web, CLI, and future clients.

Barkpark already has the hard parts: secure device authorization, team-scoped backend contracts, manifest-driven capabilities, a useful whoami, reliable MCP transport, and a paper surface that proves live writes. The onboarding failure came from missing composition between those parts.

The highest-leverage change is to make team + instance + alias + credential + client onramp one explicit transaction. If Barkpark can produce one trustworthy receipt for that transaction—and ship the same CLI wave on Windows that the docs describe—the journey becomes both shorter and safer.
